newsitem.title: USA: Clinton committed to school repair plan - official.
newsitem.headline: Clinton committed to school repair plan - official.

text.p: The Clinton Administration does not know when it will send a multi-billion dollar school fixup proposal to the new Congress, but it remains committed to a plan, a Treasury Department official said Wednesday.
"We haven't made that determination yet," Mozelle Thompson, deputy assistant secretary for government financial policy, said about the timing. "We are trying to fashion a program as soon as we can."
Thompson said the administration may "wind up changing" some features of the President's July proposal. But the "basic principles" are "still there," he said in a Reuters interview.
Asked whether the White House will send the plan to Capitol Hill in the next year, Thompson had no comment.
Thompson briefed muni public interest groups on Tuesday on the draft program.

Clinton on July 11 proposed that the federal government give localities $5 billion over four years to help them "jump start" renovation of U.S. schools, which the General Accounting Office warned recently need extensive repair.
School districts usually raise repair dollars by selling tax-exempt bonds that pay about six percent interest.
Under Clinton's plan, the administration would subsidize construction loans by 50 percent, thus cutting a locality's bond interest rate in half to three percent, the White House said in July.
"Together with investments by states and localities, this would result in $20 billion in new resources for school modernization, a 25 percent increase over the the next four years," Clinton said.
Clinton said the administration would pay for the subsidies by auctioning part of the UHF television broadcast spectrum between channels 60 and 69, which broadcasters currently are not tapping.

But Thompson said Wednesday that drafting a bill is not easy, particularly since school repair and construction has always been a local function. "We are trying to get a handle on how localities work with states," he said.
He said yesterday's meeting with municipal groups was part of series of "roundtables" Treasury and the U.S. Education Department are holding on the initiative.
"We've gotten views on what some of the urban issues are," Thompson said, noting that the Council of Great City Schools and National League of Cities are providing input.
"We also are trying to learn more about rural school districts" and their great needs, he said.
